summary: Discovery focused on private VPC deployment options. Cypher currently runs core services in AWS us-east-1 and is evaluating Redwood Private for inference to avoid egress and meet compliance. Main concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, CIDR overlap, cross-account peering, certs/DNS, KMS, and region constraints. Next: share security pack, schedule SE deep dive, confirm pilot region and CIDRs.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-02
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Elias Park (Redwood SE), Jordan Blake (CTO, Cypher), Priya Nair (Head of Platforms), Marcus Li (Network Engineer)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE for Redwood, with Elias our SE. Jordan, Priya, Marcus, thanks for the time. We're here to understand your network and security constraints for a private deployment.

[00:25] Jordan Blake: Thanks Maya, yeah we want to see how Redwood would sit inside our VPCs. High-level: we run most infra in us-east-1, some DR in us-west-2. Primary ask is no public egress for inference payloads — all traffic should be inside our network.

[00:45] Elias Park: Got it. We do Private (VPC) deployments that can be customer-managed. The two common topologies are VPC peering cross-account into a Redwood-managed VPC, or using PrivateLink / private endpoints so traffic doesn't traverse the public internet. Do you have a preference?

[01:10] Priya Nair: We'd prefer PrivateLink if possible, because peering gets messy with CIDR overlaps and transit. Our VPCs are fairly full, lots of micro-VPCs, and we use a transit gateway in some regions.

[01:30] Marcus Li: Also we have strict egress controls — outbound to internet must go via NAT GW with proxies. We need to know if Redwood needs any outbound egress, or if everything can be routed through a private endpoint.

[01:50] Elias Park: Short answer: we can do fully private endpoints. For our Private offering we can expose an interface endpoint per AZ (AWS PrivateLink) or set up peering. If you use PrivateLink, Redwood will publish an NLB-backed endpoint and you consume it in your account — no cross-account routing needed beyond the endpoint. There's some tradeoffs: PrivateLink is simpler for CIDR overlap but you have per-endpoint IPs and ENI considerations.

[02:20] Jordan Blake: And what about region constraints? We need data residency in us-east-1 for now — that's non-negotiable.

[02:35] Maya Chen: That's fine, we support private deployments in us-east-1. For Dedicated capacity we can provision in the same region; for Private (VPC) we can deploy control plane components in Redwood's management plane but keep inference nodes inside your VPC or in a peered account within the same region.

[02:55] Priya Nair: Wait, control plane in Redwood's account — does that leak logs or PII? We need audit logs kept and some customers require zero control plane access.

[03:10] Elias Park: Right, good question. We offer a private control plane option: the control plane endpoints can be reachable only over your private network (VPN or Direct Connect). Audit logs and usage telemetry can be forwarded to your logging stack; we also support granular retention. For strictest requirements we can discuss an on-prem package where you self-host the control plane.

[03:40] Marcus Li: KMS — we need customer-managed keys so that data at rest encryption keys are under our control. Any constraints on HSMs or how keys are accessed?

[03:55] Maya Chen: We integrate with customer KMS — AWS KMS CMKs are supported. For HSM-level controls, we have options to use external HSMs or CloudHSM in your account; we'll need to map the key policies accordingly. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the pack.

[04:15] Jordan Blake: Good. Also curious about ingress — will we send data to Redwood endpoints or will Redwood pull from S3 over VPC endpoints? We prefer push into private endpoints.

[04:30] Elias Park: Both are possible. For live inference we do API endpoints over PrivateLink. For bulk/model artifacts you can use S3 with VPC endpoints (S3 gateway endpoints) and we can fetch models from an S3 bucket you expose.

[04:50] Priya Nair: About peering: we use a transit VPC with route propagation. Peering directly into a Redwood VPC might conflict with our TGW setup. Will that be a blocker?

[05:05] Elias Park: If you have TGW, the recommended pattern is PrivateLink or setting up the Redwood endpoints as attachments into the TGW. Direct peering into Redwood's VPC is possible but can be complex with transitive routing limits. We'll need your network diagram to advise.

[05:30] Jordan Blake: Understood. Latency is another concern — if we put inference in our VPC, what's the expected round-trip latency? We have latency SLOs for certain features — 50 to 150 ms per request ideally.

[05:45] Maya Chen: Latency depends on instance sizing and the model used. For examples, a Dedicated cluster in the same AZ typically gets sub-50 ms token latency for short sequences on optimized models; full round-trip for generation depends on tokens. For Private deployments inside your VPC we can get similar latency as Dedicated since the resources are co-located in region/AZ.

[06:15] Marcus Li: Any difference in security posture between Hosted and Private? Like are we losing any monitoring or losing ability to rotate keys?

[06:30] Elias Park: Private gives you more control — your VPC controls networking and key ownership. Hosted (public API) is easier to integrate but involves egress. With Private you maintain full network control and key rotation. We'll provide RBAC and SSO integrations (SAML/SCIM) so you can map teams and restrict access.

[06:55] Jordan Blake: Audit logs — can logs be pushed to our CloudWatch/ELK? We need retention for 7 years for some data flows.

[07:05] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs can be forwarded via Kinesis/Firehose or direct S3 delivery. Retention policies can be configured on your side. We'll share examples.

[07:20] Priya Nair: About deployment ownership — if we go Private, will Redwood manage the instances or do we manage patching/OS?

[07:35] Elias Park: We have two models: Redwood-managed nodes inside your VPC (we operate the inference runtime but everything is in your network), or you self-manage with our operator and images. For initial pilots we often do Redwood-managed with limited host-level access, then for stricter compliance customers we do self-hosted nodes.

[08:00] Marcus Li: For peering/IP addressing: our current production VPC is 10.0.0.0/16 and many tenant VPCs use /16s too. Overlap likely. How do you handle ENI IP exhaustion for PrivateLink?

[08:20] Elias Park: PrivateLink consumes ENIs in your subnets — you need available IPs in the subnets where endpoints are placed. If IP space is tight we can use smaller subnets or rely on peering to a dedicated account that Redwood manages inside your org (cross-account but inside your AWS org) — that avoids ENI pressure but requires opening peering. We'll include options in the diagram.

[08:45] Jordan Blake: Is there any outbound NAT from your side? We must ensure nothing hits public internet for request payloads.

[08:55] Maya Chen: For PrivateLink, requests remain within AWS' network. For control plane calls there may be calls to Redwood's control plane unless you choose private control plane or self-host. We'll design flow so that inference data does not leave your VPC.

[09:15] Priya Nair: Ok. On the compliance front — SOC 2 yes, but we also need penetration testing and a data processing addendum. Do you sign DPAs with subprocessors?

[09:30] Maya Chen: Yes, we have a standard DPA and subprocessors list. We can provide SOC 2 report and our pen test summary; for pen tests we can discuss scoping depending on deployment model.

[09:45] Marcus Li: About certificates — we need mutual TLS for service-to-service calls, or at least mTLS for control plane. Are you supporting client certs?

[09:57] Elias Park: We support mTLS for service endpoints and customer-managed certs via ACM or private CAs. We'll capture that requirement.

[10:15] Jordan Blake: Great. Let's talk scale: initial pilot 5K requests/day, eventual 1M requests/day. How do you size Dedicated vs Private?

[10:30] Elias Park: We'll run a sizing questionnaire — but ballpark, pilot can be small cluster of a few GPU instances. For 1M requests/day depends on model and concurrency; we often recommend autoscaling Dedicated with reserved baseline + burst. For Private deployments hosted inside your VPC the same autoscaling patterns apply but with reserved capacity options.

[10:55] Maya Chen: Can I ask about timeline? Are you aiming for a Q3 pilot?

[11:05] Jordan Blake: We'd like to pilot in August/September, production by Q4 if results meet cost/latency. Budget approval in late August.

[11:20] Priya Nair: One more networking detail: we have strict egress rules for downloads — any model weights pulls must come from our S3 buckets via VPC endpoint. Can Redwood pull from a private S3 or do you require you to host models?

[11:35] Elias Park: We can fetch models from your S3 via role assumption and VPC endpoints. Alternatively we can host a copy in Redwood-managed storage within the same region, but for strict compliance pulling from your S3 is preferred.

[11:55] Marcus Li: Any limits on subnet count for PrivateLink endpoints? Our subnets are small and zonal.

[12:05] Elias Park: You typically need at least one subnet per AZ where you want endpoint availability. If you want cross-AZ redundancy we recommend endpoints in 2-3 AZs. ENI consumption per endpoint is modest but multiplied by AZs — we'll provide the ENI sizing table.

[12:30] Jordan Blake: Pricing: what's the delta between Dedicated reserved and Private in our VPC?

[12:40] Maya Chen: Private in your VPC has a premium relative to hosted due to networking and isolation — depends on instance types and support level. Dedicated reserved is similar pricing to Private-managed but if you self-host there are infra ops tradeoffs. We'll send a draft pricing matrix.

[12:58] Priya Nair: Ok. Can we run a short test of connectivity? E.g., we create a PrivateLink endpoint and you confirm health checks?

[13:10] Elias Park: Yes, for pilot we'll provide endpoint details and a small test harness. We'll also run a benchmark to measure latency/throughput from your app stack to the inference endpoints.

[13:30] Jordan Blake: What security documentation will you send? I want SOC2, ISO, architecture diagram, key rotation notes, list of subprocessors, and pen test summary.

[13:45] Maya Chen: We'll package all of that and include network diagrams and a sample PrivateLink architecture.

[14:00] Maya Chen: Quick note — are there any specific approval gates: legal, infosec, procurement timelines we should know about?

[14:10] Jordan Blake: Legal reviews the DPA, infosec needs the SOC2 and network diagram, and procurement handles SOW and PO. Legal turnaround ~2 weeks once DPA is in their hands.

[14:30] Priya Nair: Also tagging: we require VPC flows logs to be enabled and retained for 180 days.

[14:40] Elias Park: We can support that and provide guidance on flow logs ingestion.

[14:55] Marcus Li: A small nit: how does KV cache persistence work? We want to ensure no long-lived user data persists beyond the request window.

[15:08] Elias Park: Our runtime manages KV caches in memory by default; for customers needing persistence controls we can disable persistent caches or set TTLs. We'll include cache behavior options in the security doc.

[15:30] Jordan Blake: Sounds good. Can you also detail the SSO/SAML flow? We'll need group sync and SCIM for provisioning devs.

[15:42] Maya Chen: Yes, we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, role mapping, and session length controls. We'll include an integration guide.

[16:00] Priya Nair: Back to routes — if we do PrivateLink, do we need route table changes?

[16:08] Elias Park: PrivateLink creates ENIs in your subnets, so no route table changes generally; peering requires route propagation changes. If you use TGW you may need to attach the endpoint subnets or configure TGW propagation. We'll check with your network team.

[16:30] Jordan Blake: On data egress charges — if we host in our VPC will there be egress charges from Redwood side? We want to avoid double billing or surprise charges.

[16:45] Maya Chen: Traffic within the same region and within AWS is typically free for PrivateLink; peering costs depend on your routing. We'll clarify pricing on egress in the pricing doc and recommend patterns to minimize costs.

[17:05] Priya Nair: One more question about certificate rotation: do you handle cert rotation or do we?

[17:15] Elias Park: We can manage certs, or you can provide certs via ACM private CA; we recommend automation via ACM for rotation.

[17:30] Jordan Blake: Great. Anything we should know about model updates and version pinning? We want deterministic outputs for tests.

[17:40] Maya Chen: You can pin model versions and we support canary rollouts. For Private deployments we can freeze model versions for the pilot window and enable controlled rollouts. We'll document runbooks.

[18:00] Marcus Li: For the pilot, we'll likely want a small GPU cluster in us-east-1 with endpoints in two AZs, hit through PrivateLink, and a benchmark script. Can Redwood run the benchmark and share results?

[18:12] Elias Park: Yes, we'll run the benchmark and provide latency, p50/p95, and cost per 1k tokens. We'll ask for sample prompts.

[18:30] Jordan Blake: Ok, scope sounds clear. Anything else from Redwood?

[18:36] Maya Chen: We'll follow up with the security pack and the pricing matrix. Elias will reach out to schedule the SE deep dive.

[18:44] Priya Nair: From our side, we'll export VPC diagrams and share CIDR ranges. Marcus will be the point for network details.

[18:55] Jordan Blake: Timeline recap — security docs by 8/4, internal approval late August, SE deep dive week of 8/9, pilot in Aug/Sept.

[19:10] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll recap in an email and attach the docs.

[47:30] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels merged, occasional mis-hearings ("KV cash" appears instead of "KV cache").
